intro: Recursion and backtracking power almost every exact combinatorial search: build a partial solution one decision at a time, immediately reject (prune) any partial choice that can never lead to a valid or optimal answer, and carefully undo state before trying the next branch. The three subtopics below form a natural progression: generating permutations/subsets under constraints (the mechanics of choose-explore-unchoose), N-Queens-style pruning (using cheap incremental checks to cut the search tree early), and meet-in-the-middle (splitting a search space too large for 2^n into two halves that are brute-forced separately and joined efficiently).

subtopics.name: Permutation & Subset Generation with Constraints
subtopics.theory:
The core pattern is choose -> explore -> un-choose (undo). You maintain a partial solution (an array being built) and, at each recursive call, try every legal next element, recurse one level deeper, then remove that element before trying the next candidate so the partial solution is byte-for-byte the same as before you tried it. For permutations you typically track a `used[]` boolean array (or, for multisets, a count array) because any unused element can go in the next position. For subsets/combinations you instead pass a `start` index and only consider elements from `start` onward, which automatically avoids generating the same subset in more than one order and keeps the recursion tree at exactly 2^n leaves rather than n! orderings of each subset.

Constraints are enforced in one of two ways: filtering (generate the full unconstrained tree and check validity only at leaves) or pruning (check the constraint incrementally, the instant a partial candidate becomes invalid, and cut that whole subtree). Pruning is almost always dramatically faster because an invalid prefix kills every extension of itself. Two pruning idioms come up constantly: (1) duplicate-skipping - sort the input, and when choosing the i-th element of a combination/permutation, skip a candidate equal to the previous sibling candidate at the *same recursion depth* (not merely equal to the previous array element) so you don't regenerate an already-explored branch; (2) partial-sum bounding - if array is sorted ascending and the running sum plus the next candidate already exceeds the target, every later (larger) candidate at this level will also fail, so you can `break` out of the loop entirely instead of just `continue`-ing.

A subtle but critical correctness point: the 'un-choose' step must exactly mirror the 'choose' step. If you decremented a count array, incrementing it back must happen after the recursive call returns and *before* the next iteration of the loop tries a different branch - otherwise state leaks between sibling branches and produces silently wrong answers rather than a crash, which is why backtracking bugs are notoriously hard to spot by inspection alone.
subtopics.recognition: Look for phrasing like 'generate/list/print all distinct permutations or subsets', 'count the number of ways to choose a subset satisfying X', or 'output every arrangement in sorted/lexicographic order'. A strong signal is that the problem wants the actual objects (not just a count derivable by a formula) and n is small enough that the object count itself is the bottleneck - typically n <= 10-12 for permutations (since n! explodes past that) and n <= 20-25 for subset enumeration (2^n). If the input can contain repeated values but the expected output has each distinct arrangement exactly once, that's the signature of needing duplicate-skip pruning rather than generate-then-deduplicate-with-a-set.
subtopics.complexity: Permutations: O(n * n!) time to generate and output all n! sequences (the extra factor of n is the cost of copying/printing each one); with k groups of duplicate elements of sizes d_1..d_k, the duplicate-skip pruning generates exactly n! / (d_1! * ... * d_k!) sequences with zero wasted work, versus generating all n! and filtering with a hash set which costs extra memory and hashing time for no benefit. Subset generation is O(2^n) in the worst case, but sum-bound pruning (breaking early once a sorted running sum exceeds the target) typically prunes whole subtrees long before the recursion reaches depth n, so real-world running time on constrained instances is usually far below the 2^n worst case even though the worst-case bound itself does not change. Space is O(n) for the recursion stack and the current partial solution, plus O(number of outputs * n) if you must store every result.

examples.title: Distinct Permutations of a Multiset
examples.problem:
You are given a string s of at most 8 lowercase letters, which may contain repeated letters. Print the number of *distinct* permutations of its characters, followed by every distinct permutation, one per line, in lexicographically sorted order (this mirrors CSES 1622 'Creating Strings').
Input: a single line containing s.
Output: first line = count of distinct permutations; each following line one permutation, in sorted order.
examples.approach: Instead of generating all 8! permutations and deduplicating with a set (wasteful and, for longer strings, infeasible), recurse directly over a count array cnt[26] of remaining letters. At each position, try every letter c with cnt[c] > 0: decrement cnt[c], append c to the current string, recurse, then pop and restore cnt[c]. Because we always iterate letters in increasing alphabetical order (0..25) and never place two equal letters through two different 'copies', each distinct permutation is produced exactly once, and iterating letters in sorted order makes the output automatically lexicographically sorted with no extra sort step needed.

examples.title: Subsets Summing to a Target (with Duplicate & Bound Pruning)
examples.problem:
Given n (1 <= n <= 15) positive integers (possibly with repeated values) and a target T, find every subset (as a set of positions, but two subsets with identical multisets of values should be printed only once) whose elements sum exactly to T. Print the number of such subsets, then each subset's values in non-decreasing order, one subset per line, with subsets themselves printed in lexicographically increasing order of their value sequences.
Input: first line 'n target'; second line n integers.
Output: first line = number of qualifying subsets; each following line lists that subset's values separated by single spaces.
examples.approach: Sort the array ascending first. Recurse with (start index, running sum): at each call, iterate i from start to n-1. Skip i if a[i] equals a[i-1] and i > start (this is the duplicate-skip rule: it only skips a repeat *at the same branching level*, so '2,2,3' can still legitimately use both 2's - it just prevents choosing the second '2' as an *alternative* first choice when the first '2' at that level was already tried and undone). Also, since the array is sorted, the moment running sum + a[i] exceeds target we can 'break' (not 'continue') because every subsequent a[i] at this level is >= the current one and would only make the sum larger. When the running sum equals target exactly, record the current partial subset as a valid answer (and continue trying to extend further branches is unnecessary here since all values are positive, so we simply return without recursing deeper).

examples.title: Permutations With No Adjacent Consecutive Values
examples.problem:
Given n (1 <= n <= 9), count and list, in lexicographic order, every permutation of 1..n such that no two *adjacent positions* in the permutation hold values that differ by exactly 1 (i.e. for every i, |p[i] - p[i+1]| != 1). This sequence of counts is OEIS A002464.
Input: a single integer n.
Output: first line = number of valid permutations; each following line lists one valid permutation's values separated by spaces, in lexicographic order.
examples.approach: This demonstrates pruning a constraint *during* construction rather than generating all n! permutations and filtering afterward. Build the permutation left to right with a standard used[] array; the only addition is a single check before descending into a branch: if the permutation is non-empty and the candidate value differs from the last placed value by exactly 1, skip it immediately - never even recurse into that subtree. Because most violations happen early (adjacent to the most recently placed element), this prunes enormous swaths of the search tree compared to checking the full permutation only once it's complete. Iterating candidate values 1..n in increasing order guarantees lexicographic output order for free.

subtopics.name: Backtracking with Pruning (N-Queens Style)
subtopics.theory:
N-Queens is the canonical demonstration that a backtracking search's *asymptotic* worst case (here, roughly n^n naive placements, or n! if you already restrict to one queen per row) is almost never what determines real running time - what matters is how cheaply you can detect that a partial placement is already doomed, and how early you can detect it. The standard trick is to never rescan the board: maintain three pieces of state incrementally as you place/remove queens row by row - a bitmask (or boolean array) of occupied columns, and two more for the two diagonal directions (indexed by row - col + offset for one diagonal family, row + col for the other). Placing a queen at (row, col) and checking whether it's legal becomes an O(1) bitwise test instead of an O(n) or O(n^2) scan of previously placed queens, and undoing a placement is the exact symmetric bitwise operation.

This generalizes beyond queens to any constraint-satisfaction backtracking: Sudoku, graph coloring, exact placement puzzles. The second major lever - beyond making each check O(1) - is *variable ordering*: instead of always filling cells/rows in a fixed order, pick the most-constrained one next (in Sudoku, the empty cell with the fewest remaining legal digits; this is the 'minimum remaining values' or MRV heuristic). Committing to the most constrained decision first fails fast when a partial assignment is invalid, and succeeds with far less branching when it's valid, because you eliminate large numbers of hopeless possibilities before they can even be explored.

Extra hard constraints (like reserved/forbidden squares in a modified N-Queens board) don't change the algorithmic shape at all - they're just one more O(1) check alongside the column/diagonal checks, folded into the same incremental validity test before you recurse. This is why 'N-Queens with obstacles' (e.g. CSES 'Chessboard and Queens') is considered only a small step up from vanilla N-Queens: there is no closed-form combinatorial shortcut anymore, so you must actually run the row-by-row backtracking with attack-set pruning rather than looking up a precomputed queens-count sequence.
subtopics.recognition: Signals: 'place k non-attacking pieces', 'no two chosen items may conflict under rule R', grid-based puzzles with row/column/box uniqueness constraints, or 'count/enumerate all valid configurations' where n is small (n <= 12-16 for full board search, fixed 9x9 for Sudoku). If a brute-force enumeration of *all* placements (ignoring constraints) would be astronomically large, but checking a *partial* placement's validity is cheap and catches violations early, that's the setup for backtracking with pruning rather than plain generate-and-test.
subtopics.complexity: Worst-case complexity is still exponential (placing n queens one per row naively considers up to n choices per row, i.e. O(n^n) before any pruning, or O(n!) once you fix 'one per row'), and this bound is unavoidable in the worst case - but pruning changes the *constant factor* by orders of magnitude in practice. For n=8 queens there are 8^8 ~ 16.7 million naive row/column assignments, but column+diagonal pruning visits only a few thousand search-tree nodes to enumerate all 92 solutions, because an attacked column/diagonal kills an entire remaining subtree the instant it's detected rather than after fully constructing an invalid board. Sudoku backtracking is exponential in the number of blank cells in the absolute worst case, but the MRV heuristic (always branching on the cell with fewest candidates) keeps typical - even 'hard' - puzzles solving in well under a second because most cells end up with only 1-2 candidates once enough digits are fixed, so the effective branching factor collapses far below 9. Space is O(n) (or O(81) for Sudoku) for the incremental attack-set/candidate-mask state plus O(depth) recursion stack.

examples.title: Counting N-Queens Solutions with Bitmask Pruning
examples.problem:
Given n (1 <= n <= 12), count the number of ways to place n non-attacking queens on an n x n chessboard (no two queens share a row, column, or diagonal).
Input: a single integer n.
Output: a single integer, the number of distinct solutions.
examples.approach: Recurse row by row, always placing exactly one queen per row. Maintain three bitmasks: `cols` (columns already used), `diag1` and `diag2` (the two diagonal families, represented so that moving to the next row is a single shift). At each row, the set of legal columns is `full & ~(cols | diag1 | diag2)` where `full` has the low n bits set - this is an O(1)-per-candidate test instead of scanning previously placed queens. For the recursive call, `cols` simply gains the new queen's bit; the two diagonal masks are updated by OR-ing in the new bit and then shifting left/right by one respectively, which is exactly how a diagonal attack 'moves over' one column as you go down one row. Iterating over the available bits with `available & -available` and clearing them one at a time enumerates all legal columns for the row without ever looping over 0..n-1 explicitly. When row reaches n, a complete valid placement has been found.

examples.title: N-Queens with Reserved Squares
examples.problem:
Given an n x n board (1 <= n <= 10) where each cell is either '.' (usable) or '*' (reserved and unusable), count the number of ways to place n mutually non-attacking queens using only usable squares (this mirrors CSES 1624 'Chessboard and Queens', generalized to arbitrary n). Because some usable configurations are now forbidden there is no closed-form queens-count shortcut - you must run real backtracking.
Input: first line n; next n lines each a string of n characters ('.' or '*').
Output: a single integer, the number of valid placements.
examples.approach: This is the same row-by-row backtracking as vanilla N-Queens, with one extra O(1) check folded into the same loop: before checking column/diagonal availability for candidate column c in the current row, first check `grid[row][c] != '*'`. If the square is reserved, skip it immediately without touching any state - it never even becomes a candidate branch. Column and diagonal state are tracked with boolean arrays here (rather than bitmasks) for clarity; `diag1` is indexed by `row - c + n - 1` and `diag2` by `row + c`, the two standard ways to give every diagonal a unique, collision-free index. Marking state on entry and precisely un-marking the same three flags on return from the recursive call is what makes sibling branches see a clean board.

examples.title: Sudoku Solver with Most-Constrained-Cell Pruning
examples.problem:
Given a 9x9 Sudoku board with some cells filled (digits '1'-'9') and the rest blank ('.'), fill in the blanks so every row, column, and 3x3 box contains each digit 1-9 exactly once. The input is guaranteed to have a unique solution.
Input: 9 lines, each a string of 9 characters ('.' or a digit).
Output: 9 lines, the solved board in the same format (digits only, no dots).
examples.approach: Maintain three bitmasks per row, column, and 3x3 box recording which digits are already used (bit d set means digit d is taken). Naively picking the next blank cell in reading order and trying all 9 digits is *correct* but can be slow on harder boards because early wrong guesses aren't detected until deep into the recursion. Instead, before each recursive step, scan all blank cells once to find the one with the *fewest* remaining legal candidates (`rowMask[r] | colMask[c] | boxMask[box]` complemented and popcounted) - the 'most constrained variable' heuristic. If any blank cell has zero legal candidates, that whole branch is dead and we return false immediately (this is the pruning: we detect infeasibility without exploring further). Otherwise we branch only over that one cell's few candidates, place a digit, update the three masks, recurse, and if the recursion fails, undo the exact same three masks before trying the next candidate digit.

subtopics.name: Meet in the Middle
subtopics.theory:
Meet in the middle applies when a problem naturally wants a full O(2^n) (or O(3^n), etc.) search over subsets/assignments, n is too large for that (say n = 30-40) but small enough that half of it is trivially brute-forceable, and there is no polynomial DP shortcut - commonly because the DP state (e.g. a sum) ranges over values far too large to index into an array (weights up to 1e9, so a subset-sum DP table of that size is impossible). The technique: split the n elements into two halves of size ~n/2, recursively/iteratively brute-force *each half independently* to enumerate every possible partial result for that half (e.g. every subset sum of the left half, and every subset sum of the right half), and then combine the two result lists efficiently - typically by sorting one list and using binary search, two pointers, or a hash map against the other list - rather than trying every left-half-result paired with every right-half-result, which would just reintroduce an O(2^n) cost.

The combine step is where the real design work happens, and it depends entirely on what you're optimizing. For 'does some subset sum exactly to target T', sort the right half's sums and, for each left-half sum L, binary-search for `target - L` in the right half. For 'maximize (sum) mod m', sort the right half's sums mod m and, for each left-half value a, the maximum of `(a + b) mod m` over all right-half b is achieved either by the largest b with `a + b < m` (no wraparound) or by the single largest b overall (which may wrap around past m) - so only two binary-search queries per left value are needed, not a full scan. For k-way partitions (e.g. splitting into 3 groups rather than 2), the same idea generalizes: each half recursively enumerates all 3^(n/2) assignments instead of 2^(n/2), and the combine step must be re-derived based on how a left-half assignment and a right-half assignment jointly determine the final objective.

Correctness pitfall to watch for: always include the empty selection (contributing 0) when enumerating a half's subset sums unless the problem explicitly forbids the empty subset - it's easy to accidentally start subset masks at 1 instead of 0 and silently lose valid answers that use only elements from one half.
subtopics.recognition: Look for n roughly in the 30-40 range - too big for O(2^n) (2^40 is ~10^12, far too slow) but such that 2^(n/2) (~2^20, about a million) comfortably fits a time limit - combined with large value ranges that rule out a sum-indexed DP table (e.g. 'weights up to 10^9'), and a request to find/count/optimize something over *all subsets or assignments* rather than something with polynomial substructure. If you catch yourself thinking 'I'd brute force this with 2^n but n is just a bit too big, and DP on the sum won't fit in memory', that is exactly the meet-in-the-middle setup.
subtopics.complexity: Generating all subset results for each half costs O(2^(n/2)) time and space per half. Sorting one half's results costs O(2^(n/2) * (n/2)). The combine step is typically O(2^(n/2) log(2^(n/2))) (one binary search per element of the other half), so overall time is roughly O(n * 2^(n/2)) and space is O(2^(n/2)). This is a massive practical improvement over O(2^n): for n=40, 2^(n/2) = 2^20 ~ 1.05 million versus 2^40 ~ 1.1 trillion - the difference between finishing instantly and never finishing, even though both are technically exponential in n. The trade-off is O(2^(n/2)) memory to hold one half's enumerated results, which is the usual limiting factor rather than time.

examples.title: Counting Subsets That Sum to a Target
examples.problem:
Given n integers (1 <= n <= 36, values up to 10^9, so no sum-indexed DP is feasible) and a target sum S, count how many subsets (distinguished by which indices are chosen, so two subsets with the same values at different positions both count) sum exactly to S.
Input: first line 'n target'; second line the n integers.
Output: a single integer, the number of subsets summing to target.
examples.approach: Split the array into a left half (first n/2 elements) and a right half (remaining elements). Enumerate all 2^(|left|) subset sums of the left half by iterating every bitmask, and likewise all 2^(|right|) subset sums of the right half (including the empty subset, sum 0, in both). Sort the right half's sums. Then, for every left-half sum L, the number of right-half subsets that complete it to exactly `target` is the count of right-half sums equal to `target - L`, found via `equal_range` (binary search) on the sorted right array in O(log(2^(|right|))) time - handling duplicate sums correctly by counting the whole matching range, not just checking membership. Summing this count over every left-half sum gives the total number of subsets.

examples.title: Maximum Subsequence Sum Modulo m
examples.problem:
Given n integers (1 <= n <= 35, values up to 10^9) and a modulus m, choose any subsequence (possibly empty) to maximize (sum of chosen elements) mod m (this mirrors Codeforces 888E 'Maximum Subsequence'). n rules out both 2^n brute force and a sum-indexed DP.
Input: first line 'n m'; second line the n integers.
Output: a single integer, the maximum achievable value of (subset sum) mod m.
examples.approach: Split into two halves and enumerate every subset sum of each half (raw integer sums, not yet reduced mod m, via brute-force bitmask iteration over each half separately - each half is small enough for 2^(n/2) enumeration). Reduce the right half's sums mod m and sort them. For every left-half raw sum, reduce it mod m to get `a`, then find the best complementary right-half value `b` in O(log) time via two candidate queries: (1) the largest right-half `b` with `a + b <= m - 1` (found with `upper_bound` on `m - 1 - a`, then stepping back one), which avoids wraparound so the mod result is simply `a + b`; and (2) the single largest right-half value overall, in case `a` plus that maximum wraps around past `m` and still yields a large remainder. Because the empty subset (sum 0) is always among the enumerated sums, candidate (1) always has at least one valid match. Taking the best of both candidates across all left-half values gives the global maximum.
